I - Introduction to Variant Calling¶

1. Goal of variant calling¶

Variant calling is the automated detection of variants (SNVs, small Indels) from a file containing aligned sequencing data (BAM file).
The goal is to produce a VCF file (more details on the VCF format).

For each position of the reference genome, the algorithms (the "variant callers") take into account the counts of each allele present in the reads aligned at that position, as well as the various scores (base quality, mapping quality), to make a hypothesis about the presence of a variant and about the most likely genotype.

Sounds simple, but it actually involves several difficulties.

2. Choosing the variant caller¶

The choice of variant caller depends on the biological question / the organism studied.
Commonly found in the literature:

  • GATK Haplotype Caller or GATK Mutect2 (dedicated to tumour or mitochondrial genomes)
  • Samtools mpileup followed by Bcftools or VarScan2 (cancer-oriented)
  • FreeBayes
  • DiscoSnp (variant calling without a reference genome)
  • DeepVariant: variant calling using deep learning (complex regions, low depth)
  • Snippy: dedicated to haploid organisms.
⚠️Warning:
No tool is perfect: the quality of the calling depends on the whole pipeline, the data analysed, and the parameters used to filter the results.

91.7% concordance between Freebayes, Samtools, GATK HC (Hwang et al., 2015).
Other analyses show lower rates, 70% (O’Rawe et al., Genome Med, 2013), 57% (Cornish et al., BioMed, 2015).

3. Difficulties / Limitations¶

Many false positive variants can arise from the previous steps:

  • Read errors during “BaseCalling”
  • Artefacts related to the sequencing technology (PacBio, HiSeq, NextSeq, … )
  • Artefacts from PCR cycles during sample preparation
  • Alignment difficulties (repeated DNA regions)

Summary

  • Variant detection identifies SNVs and small Indels from an alignment file in BAM format.
  • Many tools exist for variant detection; their efficiency depends on many parameters (mapping, data quality, result filtering parameters).

II - Variant calling with the GATK suite (Genome Analysis ToolKit)¶

GATK is a suite of tools developed by the Broad Institute:

  • It comes with good documentation including various best Practices.
    • ⚠️Warning:
    The documentation may evolve a little more slowly than the versions, and some options are only documented in the command-line help.
  • It includes a local reassembly and realignment step for indels to better distinguish error sources from true variants.
  • It uses a Bayesian algorithm (statistical models to estimate the probability of each possible genotype, taking into account the various biases that can introduce noise into the data).
  • It supports the analysis of multiple samples in several batches (gVCF format).

Let's load the GATK module and create a new directory for the results.

In [ ]:
module load gatk4/4.6.1.0
mkdir -p Results/Variant_calling/

1. Genome indexing¶

Like other callers, GATK needs indexes of the reference genome to work:

  • .fai : the fasta index is a general-purpose index required by many different tools
  • .dict : the sequence dictionary is specific to the GATK suite.

Creating the fasta index: .fai (samtools)

Identify and load the samtools module

In [ ]:
module load samtools/1.23.1

Display the help of the samtools faidx command and apply it to our reference genome (fasta file).

In [ ]:
samtools faidx data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.fasta

2. BaseRecalibrator¶

Each base of a sequencing read is associated with a quality score (Phred), meant to reflect the probability that the sequencer made a mistake at that position (Q30 ↔ 1 error in 1000 bases, Q20 ↔ 1 error in 100, ...).

In practice, this score "reported" by the sequencer is only an estimate, computed by the machine's proprietary software from raw signals (intensities, phasing...). This estimate is systematically biased by technical factors, in particular:

  • the sequencing cycle (errors often increase towards the end of the read);
  • the dinucleotide context (some motifs are more error-prone, e.g. homopolymers);
  • the machine/run used (each platform has its own error signature).
⚠️Warning
Variant callers use these quality scores directly to compute the likelihood of each possible genotype.
If the reported score is too optimistic (reported quality > actual quality), we risk overestimating the confidence in false variations and therefore generating false positives.
Conversely, a score that is too pessimistic can cause true variants to be missed (false negatives).

BaseRecalibrator corrects this bias empirically.
It compares the observed bases at positions of the genome assumed to be non-variant (and therefore, in theory, sequencing errors) and builds a statistical model linking reported quality, cycle, sequence context and machine to a recalculated empirical quality.
ApplyBQSR then applies this model to correct the quality scores of each base in the BAM.

ℹ️ Note
So as not to confuse true biological variants with sequencing noise, the tool needs to exclude positions already known to be variant: this is the role of the known variant files already available in the data/genome directory:
  • Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_known_snps.vcf.gz
  • Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_known_indels.vcf.gz

Let's create a first sub-directory for the results.

In [ ]:
mkdir -p Results/Variant_calling/BaseRecalibration

BaseRecalibrator: building the recalibration model

To access the help (often very long) of GATK tools, use:

  • in the Terminal gatk TOOL_NAME --help
  • and/or the online help

For BaseRecalibrator, the command pattern is:

Usage : gatk BaseRecalibrator --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
   --input my_reads.bam \
   --reference reference.fasta \
   --known-sites sites_of_variation.vcf \
   --known-sites another/optional/setOfSitesToMask.vcf \
   --output recal_data.table

And the option we are interested in:

  • --intervals,-L : (saves time here)
    One or more genomic intervals over which to operate This argument may be specified 0 or more times, format : Chr:start-stop

Let's apply this command to our sample milca_40995, using the two known variant sets available in the data/genome/ folder and on a region of chromosome 2: NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000

In [ ]:
 gatk BaseRecalibrator --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
   --input Results/Alignment/milca_40995_md.bam \
   --reference data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.fasta \
   --known-sites data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_known_snps.vcf.gz \
   --known-sites data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_known_indels.vcf.gz \
   --intervals "NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000" \
   --output Results/Variant_calling/BaseRecalibration/milca_40995_recal.table

ApplyBQSR: applying the correction to the BAM

To access the help (often very long) of GATK tools, use:

  • in the Terminal gatk TOOL_NAME --help
  • and/or the online help

For ApplyBQSR, the command pattern is:

Usage : gatk ApplyBQSR --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
   --reference reference.fasta \
   --input input.bam \
   --bqsr-recal-file recalibration.table \
   --output output_recal.bam

And the option we are interested in:

  • --intervals,-L : (saves time here)
    One or more genomic intervals over which to operate This argument may be specified 0 or more times, format : Chr:start-stop

Let's apply this command to our sample milca_40995 and on a region of chromosome 2: NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000

In [ ]:
 gatk ApplyBQSR --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
   --input Results/Alignment/milca_40995_md.bam \
   --reference data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.fasta \
   --bqsr-recal-file Results/Variant_calling/BaseRecalibration/milca_40995_recal.table \
   --intervals "NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000" \
   --output Results/Variant_calling/BaseRecalibration/milca_40995_recal.bam

3. Variant calling and genotyping¶

3.1 Calling strategies¶

GATK offers two tools for variant calling:

  • HaplotypeCaller for germline variants. We will focus on this tool
  • Mutect2 for somatic or mitochondrial variants.

For HaplotypeCaller you have several strategies for processing samples to obtain a multi-sample VCF file.

Direct VCF output

HaplotypeCaller takes into account all the samples of your cohort at once to identify variants AND genotype the samples.

This strategy is valid if

  • you do not expect to add samples to your cohort.
  • you have few samples.
ℹ️ Note
This is the historical HaplotypeCaller method, but GVCF mode is now preferred ...

Indirect output via gVCFs

Generating gVCFs is useful because:

  • it gives the genotype at every position
  • it allows the variant panel to evolve as new samples are added, without redoing the calling on the previous samples
ℹ️ Note
This is now the recommended HaplotypeCaller method.

This 3-step procedure is suitable if you have few samples and/or you work on a small genome.

Indirect output via gVCF and GenomicDBs

Here we keep the advantages of gVCFs while optimising computing resources.

This 5-step procedure is suitable for projects with a large number of samples and/or on a large genome.

💡 Tip
You will find the details of the 5-step procedure in Annexe2_GenomicsDB.ipynb for the analysis of a large genome and/or a large cohort.

To access the help (often very long) of GATK tools, use:

  • in the Terminal gatk TOOL_NAME --help
  • and/or the online help

For HaplotypeCaller, the command pattern is:

Usage : gatk HaplotypeCaller --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
   --input input.bam [--input input2.bam] \
   --reference reference.fasta \
   --output output.vcf or output.g.vcf

HaplotypeCaller offers a great many options, but default values already exist for them and are valid in the vast majority of cases.
We will use the default values, but we recommend that you specify them in your command line so that you never forget to check them.

Here is the list of the main options:

  • --base-quality-score-threshold : Default value: 18.
    Base qualities below this threshold will be reduced to the minimum (6)
  • --min-base-quality-score,-mbq : Default value: 10.
    Minimum base quality required to consider a base for calling.
ℹ️ Note
These two options work together. The first transforms the qualities, the second is a threshold for consideration in the calling.
Here this ultimately means that only bases with a quality >= 18 will be taken into account
  • --minimum-mapping-quality : Default value: 20.
    Minimum mapping quality to keep (inclusive).
ℹ️ Note
Missing from the online documentation ...
  • --emit-ref-confidence,-ERC : Default value: NONE.
    Mode for emitting reference confidence scores (For Mutect2, this is a BETA feature).
    NONE : Regular calling without emitting reference confidence calls; BP_RESOLUTION : Reference model emitted site by site;
    GVCF : Reference model emitted with condensed non-variant blocks, i.e. the GVCF format.
ℹ️ Note
We will first use the NONE mode and then the GVCF mode.
  • --sample-ploidy,-ploidy : Default value: 2.
    Ploidy (number of chromosomes) per sample. For pooled data, set to (Number of samples in each pool * Sample Ploidy).
  • --standard-min-confidence-threshold-for-calling,-stand-call-conf : Default value: 30.0.
    The minimum phred-scaled confidence threshold at which variants should be called.
⚠️Warning
When running in `-ERC GVCF` or `-ERC BP_RESOLUTION` modes, the confidence threshold is automatically set to 0. The threshold can be set manually to the desired level in the next step of the workflow (GenotypeGVCFs)
  • --native-pair-hmm-threads : Default value: 4
    How many threads should a native pairHMM implementation use.

And other options that may interest you:

  • --mapping-quality-threshold-for-genotyping : Default value: 20.
    Control the threshold for discounting reads from the genotyper due to mapping quality after the active region detection and assembly steps but before genotyping. NOTE: this is in contrast to the --minimum-mapping-quality argument which filters reads from all parts of the HaplotypeCaller. If you would like to call genotypes with a different threshold both arguments must be set.
  • --pcr-indel-model : Default value: CONSERVATIVE.
    When calculating the likelihood of variants, we can try to correct for PCR errors that cause indel artifacts. The PCR indel model to use. Possible values: {NONE, HOSTILE, AGGRESSIVE, CONSERVATIVE}
⚠️Very important: when using PCR-free sequencing data we definitely recommend setting this argument to NONE.
  • --intervals,-L :
    One or more genomic intervals over which to operate This argument may be specified 0 or more times, format : Chr:start-stop. Here "NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000"
  • --exclude-intervals,-XL :
    One or more genomic intervals to exclude from processing This argument may be specified 0 or more times.
  • --bam-output,-bamout :
    File to which assembled haplotypes should be written.

To sum up, we will use the following command pattern:

For HaplotypeCaller, the command pattern is:
Usage : gatk HaplotypeCaller --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
            --input input.bam [--input input2.bam] \
            --reference reference.fasta \
            --intervals "NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000" \
            --base-quality-score-threshold 18 \
            --min-base-quality-score 10 \
            --minimum-mapping-quality 20 \
            -stand-call-conf 30 \
            --sample-ploidy 2 \
            --native-pair-hmm-threads 4 \
            --output output_vcf_or_g.vcf
💡 Tip
To save disk space you can add .gz to the names of your output VCF files so that they are automatically compressed.
In that case, to browse your file use the command zcat FILE.vcf.gz | more (or less)

3.2 GATK with VCF output (--emit-ref-confidence NONE)¶

Reminder: this mode of use is worthwhile when:

  • you do not expect to add samples to your cohort.
  • you have few samples

Let's browse the output file with the more or less command in your Terminal.

A VCF file always contains a header, then a file "body" structured in 9 columns, followed by one column per sample.
The content of these columns can however vary depending on the variant caller used.

The GATK page dedicated to the VCF format covers these different sections/columns.

3.3 GATK with GVCF output (--emit-ref-confidence GVCF)¶

Reminder:
The analysis process to obtain a multi-sample VCF is done in several steps and depends on the size of your genome and of your sampling:

  • 3-step strategy if you have few samples and/or you work on a small genome:
    • HaplotypeCaller in GVCF mode on each sample
    • CombineGVCFs to obtain a multi-sample GVCF
    • GenotypeGVCFs to convert your multi-sample GVCF file into a multi-sample VCF.

This is the process we are going to see in the practical session.

  • 5-step strategy, if you have a large number of samples and/or you work on a large genome:
    • HaplotypeCaller in GVCF mode on each sample (one gVCF per sample, as before)
    • SplitIntervals to split the genome into intervals that will allow the following steps to be parallelised over sub-regions of balanced size.
    • GenomicsDBImport, run on each interval, to import all the individual gVCFs into a GenomicsDB workspace specific to that interval.
    • GenotypeGVCFs, run on each GenomicsDB workspace (one per interval), to produce one multi-sample VCF per interval.
    • GatherVcfs to concatenate the VCFs obtained on each interval from the same set of samples.

💡 Tip
You will find the details of the 5-step procedure in Annexe2_GenomicsDB.ipynb for the analysis of a large genome and/or a large cohort.

Back to the 3-step procedure: let's start by creating a new results directory

In [ ]:
mkdir -p Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode
a) HaplotypeCaller in gvcf mode¶

Here, for each sample, we seek to genotype every position of the genome (or of the interval if specified).

Run HaplotypeCaller as before, still on the interval NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000 to save time:

  • on one sample: Results/Variant_calling/BaseRecalibration/milca_40995_recal.bam
  • changing the option to --emit-ref-confidence GVCF
  • changing the output file
💡 Tip (reminder)
As before, add .gz to the names of your output gVCF files so that they are automatically compressed.
In that case, to browse your file use the command zcat FILE.vcf.gz | more (or less)
In [ ]:
gatk HaplotypeCaller --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
    --input Results/Variant_calling/BaseRecalibration/milca_40995_recal.bam \
    --reference data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.fasta \
    --intervals "NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000" \
    --base-quality-score-threshold 18 \
    --min-base-quality-score 10 \
    --minimum-mapping-quality 20 \
    --sample-ploidy 2 \
    --emit-ref-confidence GVCF \
    --native-pair-hmm-threads 4 \
    --output Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/milca_40995.g.vcf

Let's browse the output file with the more or less command in your Terminal.

The gVCF file and the VCF file have many similarities. They contain a header, then a file "body" structured in 9 columns, followed by one column per sample.

On the GATK website, you will find a page dedicated to the GVCF format

Header lines start with ##. To display the first lines of the file "body", use the grep command with the -v option to ignore this ## pattern.

In [ ]:
grep -v "##" Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/milca_40995.g.vcf | head

Question
  • While we are trying to get the genotype at every position, why do we jump from position 90000000 to position 90000028?
  • Apart from the positions and the reference alleles (REF), what differentiates these lines?

b) CombineGVCFs¶

This second step consists in aggregating the samples, still over all the positions of the genome (or of the interval).
It produces a multi-sample gVCF file.

For CombineGVCFs, the command pattern is:

Usage : gatk CombineGVCFs --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
   --reference reference.fasta \
   --variant sample1.g.vcf.gz \
   --variant sample2.g.vcf.gz \
   --output cohort.g.vcf.gz

The only option we are interested in is:

  • --intervals : One or more genomic intervals over which to operate This argument may be specified 0 or more times, format: CHR:start-stop

Run CombineGVCFs on our 4 samples and on the interval NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000.

In [ ]:
gatk CombineGVCFs --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
    --variant   Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/milca_40995.g.vcf \
    --variant   Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/milca_40998.g.vcf \
    --variant   Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/control_41011.g.vcf \
    --variant   Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/control_41012.g.vcf \
    --reference data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.fasta \
    --intervals "NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000" \
    --output    Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/4samples_selected_region.g.vcf

c) GenotypeGVCFs¶

This last step consists in detecting the variants and genotyping them across all samples. It produces a multi-sample VCF file.

For GenotypeGVCFs, the command pattern is:

Usage : gatk GenotypeGVCFs --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
   --reference reference.fasta \
   --variant multi-sample.g.vcf.gz \
   --output cohort.vcf.gz

Les options qui nous intéressent sont :

  • --intervals,-L:
    One or more genomic intervals over which to operate This argument may be specified 0 or more times, format : Chr:start-stop. Ici "NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000"
  • --standard-min-confidence-threshold-for-calling,-stand-call-conf : Default value: 30.0.
    The minimum phred-scaled confidence threshold at which variants should be called.

Run GenotypeGVCFs on our multi-sample GVCF and on the interval NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000.

In [ ]:
gatk GenotypeGVCFs --java-options '-Xmx8G' \
    --reference data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.fasta  \
    --variant   Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/4samples_selected_region.g.vcf \
    -stand-call-conf 30 \
    --intervals "NC_037329.1:90000000-91140000" \
    --output    Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/4samples_selected_region.vcf

3.4 Brief comparison¶

The annotation step that follows will give us many details on the number and type of variants we have been able to detect.

Here, let's simply check the number of variants (number of lines) included in each of our callings (1-step VCF mode or 3-step gVCF mode).

As a reminder, VCFs contain many header lines starting with #. To get the number of variants we can:

  • search for all lines that do not contain # with the grep command
  • count the number of remaining lines with the wc -l command
In [ ]:
grep -v "#" Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_vcf_mode/4samples_selected_region.vcf |wc -l

grep -v "#" Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/4samples_selected_region.vcf |wc -l

4272
6653

IV - Variant Annotation¶

The goal of this annotation is to add biological information to the variants:

  • are these variants already known?
  • what do we know about the regions in which they are located? This is called structural annotation.

The goal of this annotation is to add biological information to the variants:

  • are these variants already known?
  • what do we know about the regions in which they are located? This is called structural annotation.
  • can we predict the impact of each allele? This is called functional annotation.

Several tools and variant databases can be used to perform this annotation. These include:

  • Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (Ensembl VEP)
  • the SnpEff/SnpSift tool suite

For this practical session, we focus on the SnpEff / SnpSift tool suite:

  • SnpEff predicts the functional effect of variants: from a VCF and a genomic annotation database (positions of genes, exons, introns, transcripts), it determines for each variant which genic context it falls in, and predicts its impact on the protein. This functional annotation is added to the INFO field of each variant.
  • SnpSift is the companion tool for filtering, manipulation and additional annotation. It can filter variants using logical expressions on any INFO/FORMAT field, and cross them with known annotation databases.

Let's load the first module, SnpEff, and create a new results directory.

In [ ]:
module load snpeff/5.2
mkdir Results/Variant_annotation/

1. Building the annotation database¶

To annotate variants, SnpEff needs a reference database of the genic context of the studied genome.

Many genomes (> 20,000) are already indexed.
You can find the list with the snpEff databases command followed by the grep command to sub-select lines with a keyword, here (Bos_taurus).

In [ ]:
snpEff databases | grep Bos_taurus

If your genome exists, you can use the snpEff download command

The command pattern is:

Usage: snpEff download [options] genome_version

and the option you are interested in is:

  • -dataDir : to specify where you want to store the database.
⚠️ Warning
Use an absolute path for this parameter, otherwise it will be relative to the configuration file⚠️

example:

snpEff download -dataDir /shared/projects/2621_eb3in1_2026/atelier_variant/TP_small_variants/data/genome/snpeff_db ARS-UCD1.2.105
# or
snpEff download -dataDir `pwd`/data/genome/snpeff_db ARS-UCD1.2.105

The ARS-UCD2.0 version of the cattle genome is not available. We therefore need to build our own reference database, at a minimum from:

  • the fasta file of your genome (Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.fasta)
  • the GFF annotation file (Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.gff).

and optionally from:

  • the CDS fasta file
  • the protein fasta file
  • gff or bed files of regulatory regions or transcription factor motifs (from Ensembl: https://regulation.ensembl.org/)
  • the pdb file of protein interactions (from PDB or AlphaFold)
  • any other .bed file of regions of interest (these will be used at annotation time)

For more details see the online documentation.

⚠️ Warning
Some of this information comes from Ensembl, so you must have used an Ensembl reference during your sequence analysis.

Let's start by creating a snpeff_db directory in our data/genome directory.

In [ ]:
mkdir data/genome/snpeff_db

Choose a prefix that will identify your genome in the SnpEff config file and will be used to create the directory that will contain the associated annotation database.

💡 Tip
choose a name that is as explicit as possible, for example here: Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual
  • Copy the original snpEff configuration file (/shared/software/miniconda_deployment//envs/snpeff-5.2/share/snpeff-5.2-3/snpEff.config) into your new directory (data/genome/snpeff_db)
In [ ]:
cp /shared/software/miniconda_deployment//envs/snpeff-5.2/share/snpeff-5.2-3/snpEff.config data/genome/snpeff_db/snpeff.config

Open it with the Jupyter file browser.

Scroll down to the section that tells you how to add a new genome (lines 128 - 131).

# For genome version 'ZZZ' the entries look like
#	ZZZ.genome              : Real name for ZZZ (e.g. 'Human')
#	ZZZ.reference           : [Optional] Comma separated list of URL to site/s where information for building ZZZ database was extracted.
#	ZZZ.chrName.codonTable  : [Optional] Define codon table used for chromosome 'chrName' (Default: 'codon.Standard')

Add a section after it (for example at line 134) for our genome, replacing ZZZ with our prefix Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual.

ℹ️ Note
  • the ZZZ.reference line indicates where to download the data. This does not concern us
  • the ZZZ.chrName.codonTable line lets you indicate whether a sequence (chrName) of your genome uses different codons (see lines 86 to 122).
    This is the case, for example, of the mitochondrion. This does not concern us either.

ℹ️ Note
Start your lines with a # if you want to add a comment.

For example:

#---
# Manual Databases
#---

# Chr2 and 6 of the Bos taurus ARS-UCD2.0 genome
Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual.genome : Bovine (ARS-UCD2.0 extracted for the Roscoff practical session)
  • Create the <prefix> directory (i.e. data/genome/snpeff_db/Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual) to store the SnpEff annotation database
In [ ]:
mkdir -p data/genome/snpeff_db/Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual
  • Copy the genome sequences under the name sequences.fa and the annotations under the name genes.gff into the previous directory
In [ ]:
cp data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.fasta data/genome/snpeff_db/Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual/sequences.fa
cp data/genome/Bos_taurus_GCF_002263795.3_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6.gff data/genome/snpeff_db/Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual/genes.gff

Check the contents of the genome folder with the tree command

In [ ]:
tree data/genome/snpeff_db

data/genome/snpeff_db
├── Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual
│   ├── genes.gff
│   └── sequences.fa
└── snpeff.config

1 directory, 3 files

To build the database, we are going to use the snpEff build tool.
To display the help use the -h option or consult the online documentation.

In [ ]:
snpEff build -h

snpEff version SnpEff 5.2 (build 2023-09-29 06:17), by Pablo Cingolani
Usage: snpEff build [options] genome_version

Build DB options:

Database format option (default: Auto detect):
	-embl                        : Use Embl format.
	-genbank                     : Use GenBank format.
	-gff2                        : Use GFF2 format (obsolete).
	-gff3                        : Use GFF3 format.
	-gtf22                       : Use GTF 2.2 format.
	-knowngenes                  : Use KnownGenes table from UCSC.
	-refseq                      : Use RefSeq table from UCSC.

Database build options:
	-cellType <type>             : Only build regulation tracks for cellType <type>.
	-maxErrorRate <num>          : Maximum allowed error rate (number between 0.0 and 1.0). Default: 0.05
	-noCheckCds                  : Skip CDS sequences check.
	-noCheckProtein              : Skip Protein sequences check.
	-noStoreSeqs                 : Do not store sequence in binary files. Default: false
	-onlyReg                     : Only build regulation tracks.
	-regSortedByType             : The 'regulation.gff' file is sorted by 'regulation type' instead of sorted by chromosome:pos. Default: false
	-storeSeqs                   : Store sequence in binary files. Default: true

Generic options:
	-c , -config                 : Specify config file
	-configOption name=value     : Override a config file option
	-d , -debug                  : Debug mode (very verbose).
	-dataDir <path>              : Override data_dir parameter from config file.
	-download                    : Download a SnpEff database, if not available locally. Default: true
	-nodownload                  : Do not download a SnpEff database, if not available locally.
	-h , -help                   : Show this help and exit
	-noLog                       : Do not report usage statistics to server
	-q , -quiet                  : Quiet mode (do not show any messages or errors)
	-v , -verbose                : Verbose mode
	-version                     : Show version number and exit

























The command pattern is:


Usage: snpEff build [options] genome_version



and the options we are interested in are:


    

  • -gff3 : which indicates the annotation format (even though there is an auto-detect mode by default)
    • 

  • -noCheckCds : because we do not have a CDS fasta file
    • 

  • -noCheckProtein : because we do not have a protein fasta file
    • 

  • -c : to specify our configuration file
    • 

  • -dataDir : to specify where you want to store the database.
    • 

    
    ⚠️ Warning
    
    Use an absolute path for this parameter, otherwise it will be relative to the configuration file

    

  • -v, -verbose : to get, among other things, a summary of the genic information taken into account.
    • 























Apply this pattern to the previously prepared files.


















In [ ]:






snpEff build -gff3 -noCheckCds -noCheckProtein -c data/genome/snpeff_db/snpeff.config -dataDir `pwd`/data/genome/snpeff_db -v Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual

2. Annotation with our database¶






















We are now going to annotate our multi-sample VCF file with the snpEff eff tool.


To display the help use the -h option or consult the online help.


















In [ ]:






snpEff eff -h

























snpEff version SnpEff 5.2 (build 2023-09-29 06:17), by Pablo Cingolani
Usage: snpEff [eff] [options] genome_version [input_file]


	variants_file                   : Default is STDIN



Options:
	-chr <string>                   : Prepend 'string' to chromosome name (e.g. 'chr1' instead of '1'). Only on TXT output.
	-classic                        : Use old style annotations instead of Sequence Ontology and Hgvs.
	-csvStats <file>                : Create CSV summary file.
	-download                       : Download reference genome if not available. Default: true
	-i <format>                     : Input format [ vcf, bed ]. Default: VCF.
	-fileList                       : Input actually contains a list of files to process.
	-o <format>                     : Ouput format [ vcf, gatk, bed, bedAnn ]. Default: VCF.
	-s , -stats, -htmlStats         : Create HTML summary file.  Default is 'snpEff_summary.html'
	-noStats                        : Do not create stats (summary) file

Results filter options:
	-fi , -filterInterval  <file>   : Only analyze changes that intersect with the intervals specified in this file (you may use this option many times)
	-no-downstream                  : Do not show DOWNSTREAM changes
	-no-intergenic                  : Do not show INTERGENIC changes
	-no-intron                      : Do not show INTRON changes
	-no-upstream                    : Do not show UPSTREAM changes
	-no-utr                         : Do not show 5_PRIME_UTR or 3_PRIME_UTR changes
	-no <effectType>                : Do not show 'EffectType'. This option can be used several times.

Annotations options:
	-cancer                         : Perform 'cancer' comparisons (Somatic vs Germline). Default: false
	-cancerSamples <file>           : Two column TXT file defining 'oringinal \t derived' samples.
	-fastaProt <file>               : Create an output file containing the resulting protein sequences.
	-formatEff                      : Use 'EFF' field compatible with older versions (instead of 'ANN').
	-geneId                         : Use gene ID instead of gene name (VCF output). Default: false
	-hgvs                           : Use HGVS annotations for amino acid sub-field. Default: true
	-hgvsOld                        : Use old HGVS notation. Default: false
	-hgvs1LetterAa                  : Use one letter Amino acid codes in HGVS notation. Default: false
	-hgvsTrId                       : Use transcript ID in HGVS notation. Default: false
	-lof                            : Add loss of function (LOF) and Nonsense mediated decay (NMD) tags.
	-noHgvs                         : Do not add HGVS annotations.
	-noLof                          : Do not add LOF and NMD annotations.
	-noShiftHgvs                    : Do not shift variants according to HGVS notation (most 3prime end).
	-oicr                           : Add OICR tag in VCF file. Default: false
	-sequenceOntology               : Use Sequence Ontology terms. Default: true

Generic options:
	-c , -config                 : Specify config file
	-configOption name=value     : Override a config file option
	-d , -debug                  : Debug mode (very verbose).
	-dataDir <path>              : Override data_dir parameter from config file.
	-download                    : Download a SnpEff database, if not available locally. Default: true
	-nodownload                  : Do not download a SnpEff database, if not available locally.
	-h , -help                   : Show this help and exit
	-noLog                       : Do not report usage statistics to server
	-q , -quiet                  : Quiet mode (do not show any messages or errors)
	-v , -verbose                : Verbose mode
	-version                     : Show version number and exit

Database options:
	-canon                       : Only use canonical transcripts.
	-canonList <file>            : Only use canonical transcripts, replace some transcripts using the 'gene_id 	 transcript_id' entries in <file>.
	-tag <tagName>               : Only use transcript having a tag 'tagName'. This option can be used multiple times.
	-notag <tagName>             : Filter out transcript having a tag 'tagName'. This option can be used multiple times.
	-interaction                 : Annotate using interactions (requires interaction database). Default: true
	-interval <file>             : Use a custom intervals in TXT/BED/BigBed/VCF/GFF file (you may use this option many times)
	-maxTSL <TSL_number>         : Only use transcripts having Transcript Support Level lower than <TSL_number>.
	-motif                       : Annotate using motifs (requires Motif database). Default: true
	-nextProt                    : Annotate using NextProt (requires NextProt database).
	-noGenome                    : Do not load any genomic database (e.g. annotate using custom files).
	-noExpandIUB                 : Disable IUB code expansion in input variants
	-noInteraction               : Disable inteaction annotations
	-noMotif                     : Disable motif annotations.
	-noNextProt                  : Disable NextProt annotations.
	-onlyReg                     : Only use regulation tracks.
	-onlyProtein                 : Only use protein coding transcripts. Default: false
	-onlyTr <file.txt>           : Only use the transcripts in this file. Format: One transcript ID per line.
	-reg <name>                  : Regulation track to use (this option can be used add several times).
	-ss , -spliceSiteSize <int>  : Set size for splice sites (donor and acceptor) in bases. Default: 2
	-spliceRegionExonSize <int>  : Set size for splice site region within exons. Default: 3 bases
	-spliceRegionIntronMin <int> : Set minimum number of bases for splice site region within intron. Default: 3 bases
	-spliceRegionIntronMax <int> : Set maximum number of bases for splice site region within intron. Default: 8 bases
	-strict                      : Only use 'validated' transcripts (i.e. sequence has been checked). Default: false
	-ud , -upDownStreamLen <int> : Set upstream downstream interval length (in bases)





































The command pattern is:


Usage: snpEff [eff] [options] genome_version [input_file] > output_file



and the options we are interested in are:


    

  • -c : to specify our configuration file
    • 

  • -dataDir : to specify where the annotation database is stored.
    • 

    
    ⚠️ Warning
    
    Use an absolute path for this parameter, otherwise it will be relative to the configuration file

    

  • -s , -stats, -htmlStats : to specify the path of the analysis report (HTML format)
    • 























Apply this pattern to the multi-sample VCF file and write the result (a VCF) to your output directory Results/Variant_annotation/


















In [ ]:






snpEff eff -c data/genome/snpeff_db/snpeff.config \
           -dataDir `pwd`/data/genome/snpeff_db \
           -s Results/Variant_annotation/snpeff_report.html \
           Bos_taurus_ARS-UCD2.0_chr2_chr6_manual \
           Results/Variant_calling/haplotypeCaller_gvcf_mode/4samples_selected_region.vcf > Results/Variant_annotation/4samples_selected_region_annotated.vcf

The online documentation gives a detailed description of this ANN field,

and a dedicated section lists the different types of effects and their impact "strength".


To make exploring the results easier, download the snpeff_report.html file and let's explore it together.



Question

    If you had to prioritise the exploration of these variants, which ones would you choose?























3. Selecting variants of interest¶






















Exploring the annotated VCF as it is does not seem easy.


For this we are going to use a new tool, SnpSift, and its filter command.


Load the dedicated module and display the help of the SnpSift command with the -h option.


















In [ ]:






module load snpsift/4.3.1t
SnpSift filter -h

























SnpSift version 4.3t (build 2017-11-24 10:18), by Pablo Cingolani

Usage: java -jar SnpSift.jar filter [options] 'expression' [input.vcf]
Options:
	-a|--addFilter <str>  : Add a string to FILTER VCF field if 'expression' is true. Default: '' (none)
	-e|--exprFile <file>  : Read expression from a file
	-f|--file <input.vcf> : VCF input file. Default: STDIN
	-i|--filterId <str>   : ID for this filter (##FILTER tag in header and FILTER VCF field). Default: 'SnpSift'
	-n|--inverse          : Inverse. Show lines that do not match filter expression
	-p|--pass             : Use 'PASS' field instead of filtering out VCF entries
	-r|--rmFilter <str>   : Remove a string from FILTER VCF field if 'expression' is true (and 'str' is in the field). Default: '' (none)
	-s|--set <file>       : Create a SET using 'file'
	--errMissing          : Error is a field is missing. Default: false
	--format <format>     : SnpEff format version: {2, 3}. Default: Auto
	--galaxy              : Used from Galaxy (expressions have been sanitized).





































The command pattern is:


Usage:
    java -jar SnpSift.jar filter [options] 'expression' [input.vcf] > output.vcf
    # or more simply
    SnpSift filter [options] 'expression' [input.vcf] > output.vcf



SnpSift uses an expression system to select variants.
The expression can involve any of the VCF columns: CHROM, POS, ID, REF, ALT, QUAL, FILTER, INFO, FORMAT but also all the sub-fields, typically the ANN sub-field of the INFO column or the genotypes.


The online documentation gives many examples.






















For example, let's select all variants that cause an amino acid change (missense_variant)


















In [ ]:






SnpSift filter \
    "ANN[0].EFFECT has 'missense_variant'" \
    Results/Variant_annotation/4samples_selected_region_annotated.vcf \
    > Results/Variant_annotation/4samples_selected_region_missens_variant.vcf 

























Let's count the number of selected variants (selecting lines that do not start with "#" and counting)


















In [ ]:






grep -v "#" Results/Variant_annotation/4samples_selected_region_missens_variant.vcf | wc -l

























36

























As a reminder, we have:


    

  • 2 samples carrying the "milca" mutation: 40995 and 40998
    • 

  • 2 non-carrier samples: 41011 and 41012
    • 



We may then want to filter the variants that are homozygous reference in the non-carriers (0/0), and variant in the carriers (0/1 or 1/1).


















In [ ]:






SnpSift filter  \
 'isVariant( GEN[milca_40995] ) & isVariant( GEN[milca_40998] ) & isRef( GEN[control_41011] ) & isRef( GEN[control_41012] ) ' \
 Results/Variant_annotation/4samples_selected_region_missens_variant.vcf \
 > Results/Variant_annotation/4samples_selected_region_missens_variant_milca_mutation.vcf

This mutation was detected in 3.7% of Montbéliarde cattle. 

The authors of the publication also showed that the position of the variant is extremely conserved across orthologues and paralogues of the FZD gene family, which strengthens the hypothesis of a causal effect of this mutation.






















Conclusion¶






















We have seen:






















    

  • Variant calling is sensitive to many experimental and methodological factors
    • 

  • The GATK tool suite is one of the references and offers an analysis workflow that includes:
      

    • Recalibration of sequence qualities via BaseRecalibrator and ApplyBQSR
      • 

    • Variant calling, notably with HaplotypeCaller
      • 

    • Management of large sample cohorts, notably with CombineGVCFs and GenotypeGVCFs
      • 

    

    • 

  • Variant annotation includes structural and functional annotation.
    • 

  • This annotation depends on the known resources linked to your genome (⚠️beware of reference compatibility)
    • 























In addition to this material, you have two appendices:


    

  • Annexe1_Baserecalibration.ipynb for building a set of "reliable" variants allowing proper use of the base recalibration tools.
    • 

  • Annexe2_GenomicsDB.ipynb for managing large cohorts and/or analyses on large genomes by applying the 5-step calling strategy.
    •
